one_liner: C++Now/CppCon 2025 talk building a C++ DGEMM step by step to roughly OpenBLAS speed; slides only, no code.
what_it_does: Aliaksei Sala's talk 'Achieving Peak Performance for Matrix Multiplication' (C++Now 2025, repeated at CppCon 2025) takes dense square GEMM on row-major, 64-byte-aligned std::vector<double> matrices (2880 x 2880, larger than L3) from a naive triple loop through ten optimisation steps, timing each one and finishing with an OpenBLAS comparison. It is not a library: the code exists only as fragments on the slides (functions like matMul_Naive_Tile(A, B, C) and templated micro-kernels), and neither deck links a repository; the only contact given is a LinkedIn profile.
how_it_is_fast: The steps follow the Goto/BLIS recipe (the deck credits Robert van de Geijn): ikj loop order, 64-wide tiling, AVX2 FMA (_mm256_fmadd_pd), cache blocking with Mc=180, Nc=96, Kc=240, a 4x12 register block (12 ymm accumulators plus 3 for B), OpenMP over the outer blocks with pinned threads, packing B (the slides say packing A had no effect), reordering panels to unit stride, manual unrolling and _mm_prefetch with the NTA hint. The CppCon 2025 deck adds a portable kernel written with std::experimental::simd and index_sequence fold expressions (zen5_packed_kernel), a 4x8 thread grid to use 32 threads, and float and bfloat16 instantiations (bf16 through an intrinsics specialisation the slide says 'will be removed').
when_to_use: Learning or teaching how a BLIS-style GEMM is built in C++, with a measured time for every step (152 s naive down to 0.336 s on a 4-core i5-6300HQ)
Judging whether portable C++ (std::experimental::simd templates) can get close to a tuned BLAS on your CPU before committing to assembly
A design reference for a custom kernel where your BLAS lacks the type, e.g. bfloat16 GEMM on a Zen 5 desktop, which the CppCon deck says OpenBLAS did not support
when_not_to_use: Any production use: there is no repository, license, test suite or build, so you would be re-typing slide fragments; use OpenBLAS, BLIS, MKL or Eigen

Expecting a win on AVX2 machines: on the one fully specified run (i5-6300HQ, 2880^2 FP64, -O3 -march=haswell -ffast-math) OpenBLAS took 0.310 s against 0.336 s, about 8% faster (derived from page data)
Odd or non-square shapes: the slide kernels use fixed constexpr block sizes and show no edge handling, and 2880 is an exact multiple of Mc, Nc and Kc
Code that needs a BLAS interface (column-major, transposes, alpha/beta, leading dimensions); none is shown
Relying on the Zen 5 numbers: matrix size, compiler, flags and OpenBLAS version for that run are not stated in the deck

integration.dependencies: OpenMP; AVX2/FMA intrinsics in the C++Now version, std::experimental::simd (Parallelism TS v2) in the CppCon version
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; the slides use C++17 fold expressions and std::experimental::simd, and the C++Now benchmark was built with -O3 -march=haswell -ffast-math on Linux (compiler not named)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2/FMA (Skylake i5-6300HQ) and an AVX-512 Zen 5 desktop (CppCon deck); nothing else documented

gotchas: The slide 'Assembly: Where the FLOPs Really Happen / All kernels are written in assembly' describes production BLAS libraries, not this code; the talk's kernels are C++ (AVX2 intrinsics, then std::experimental::simd), and the CppCon deck concludes 'C++ can deliver assembly-class performance on matrix multiply.'

Percent-of-peak figures depend on the clock assumed: the C++Now deck uses 2.3 GHz (147.2 GFLOPS peak, so OpenBLAS shows 104%), the CppCon deck 2.8 GHz (179.2 GFLOPS); for Zen 5 it gives 2.9 TFLOPS at 5.7 GHz but expects 1.95 TFLOPS after an AVX-512 downclock to 3.8 GHz.
Built with -ffast-math, so floating-point reassociation is allowed; results need not match a strict-IEEE BLAS bit for bit.
The slides report up to 40% performance differences between Clang and GCC for intermediate versions, marked 'NOT applicable for the final version'.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Never as a dependency; as study material it complements optimize-gemm (Avafly), sgemm.c (salykova) and cpu_gemm_opt, which cover the same blocking-and-packing path but ship runnable code that beats OpenBLAS in their own runs, so use those if you want something to build.
verified_claims_summary: C++Now 2025 slides (PDF): final version 0.336 s / 142.2 GFLOPS vs OpenBLAS 0.310 s / 154.1 GFLOPS for 2880^2 FP64 on a 4-core i5-6300HQ under Linux with -O3 -march=haswell -ffast-math, so OpenBLAS is about 8% faster. CppCon 2025 deck (Keynote, text extracted): on a 16-core, 5.7 GHz Zen 5 CPU (kernel named zen5_packed_kernel; consistent with a Ryzen 9 9950X, though the slide text does not name the model) 'Matmul: 1.7 TFLOPS' vs 'Openblas: 1.58 TFLOPS' in FP64 (about 1.08x, derived from page data), a tie at 3.57 TFLOPS in FP32, and 3.09 TFLOPS in bfloat16 with no OpenBLAS counterpart; first-party, no code.
status_note: A conference talk, not a maintained project: no code, license or repository was found, so it is reference-only; the author's 'future plans' slide lists finishing the CPU work and repeating it on GPUs and AI chips.
